```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 3.8)
library(MDPL)
```

## The idea

A randomised trial gives an unbiased but noisy treatment effect;
observational data are larger but may be confounded. MDPL (*multi-source
data fusion via power likelihoods*) raises the likelihood of each
observational data set $k$ to a weight $\eta_k\in[0,1]$:

$$p(\theta \mid \text{trial}, \text{sources}) \;\propto\; L_{\text{trial}}(\theta)\prod_k L_k(\theta)^{\eta_k}.$$

The weights are chosen based on agreement with the trial data: a source
that agrees with the trial gets a weight near 1, a biased one near 0.
This holds for every model (GLMs, `causl` frugal models, your own
likelihood); only the specification changes.

Throughout the vignettes we say *observational* for the data that
supplement the trial, but nothing in the method requires them to be
observational: any secondary data (another trial, a registry, historical
controls) can be used in the same way. A *source* is any one of the
data sets, trial or secondary.

## The key functions

An analysis takes two steps:

| step | function | what it does |
|----|----|----|
| 1\. fit | `mdpl()` | fits the model to the trial and each source, chooses the weights, returns one object |
| 2\. estimate | `mdpl_cate()`, `mdpl_ate()`, `mdpl_coef()` | effects and coefficients with intervals, for any trace, scale or population |

The step 1 object already holds the weights (`fit$eta`), the
coefficients, ATE and CATE (`fit$estimates`), the fitted models and,
with `bootstrap_CI = TRUE`, the bootstrap replicates; step 2 is for
anything beyond the defaults. The **CATE** is set by the outcome model:
for `Y ~ A * X` it is the `A` coefficient plus the `A:X` coefficient
times `X`, stored as a formula you can call on any data frame of
covariates.

`mdpl()` takes the model, the trial and a *list* of observational data
sets:

``` r
mdpl(model, data_exp, data_obs, treat = "A", target = NULL,
     method = c("taylor", "elpd", "cv"), pooled = FALSE,
     bootstrap_CI = FALSE, B = 500, family = gaussian(),
     cate = TRUE, ate = TRUE, coef = TRUE)
```

- `model`: a formula (with `family` for non-Gaussian GLMs) or a
  specification object (models vignette).
- `data_exp`, `data_obs`: the trial and a named list of observational data sets;
  treatment is a 0/1 column named by `treat`.
- `target`: what the weights are judged on; default the whole parameter
  vector, `"cate"` the treatment terms only.
- `method`: `"taylor"` (fast, default), `"elpd"` or `"cv"` (weights
  vignette).
- `cate`, `ate`, `coef`: what to store in `fit$estimates` (default all);
  `cate` can also be a data frame of covariate values.
- `pooled`: one common weight for all sources.

## A simulated example

One trial ($n=300$) and three observational data sets ($n=1000$ each) with no, mild and
strong unmeasured confounding. The true effect is
$\tau(x) = 0.2 + 0.1x$.

```{r sim}
set.seed(1)
sim <- function(n, bias = 0) {
  X <- rnorm(n, 1); U <- rnorm(n)
  A <- rbinom(n, 1, if (bias == 0) 0.5 else plogis(X - 1 + bias * U))
  data.frame(X = X, A = A, Y = 0.5 + X + 0.2 * A + 0.1 * A * X + bias * U + rnorm(n))
}
trial <- sim(300)
obs <- list(clean = sim(1000, 0), mild = sim(1000, 0.5), strong = sim(1000, 2))
head(trial, 3)
```

## Fit

`Y ~ A * X` lets the effect vary with `X`; `cate = nd` also stores the
effect at `X` = 0, 1, 2. `bootstrap_CI = TRUE` refits and reselects the weights
on `B` resamples, so the intervals below allow for choosing the weights.

```{r fit}
nd <- data.frame(X = c(0, 1, 2))
fit <- mdpl(Y ~ A * X, trial, obs, treat = "A", cate = nd,
            bootstrap_CI = TRUE, B = 500, boot_seed = 1)
fit
```

## The weights

`fit$eta` has a row per source and a column per *trace multiplier*.
**`t2` (leave-one-out) is the default**; the more conservative `t1` is
available with `trace = "t1"`. A weight near 1 pools the observational data with the
trial, near 0 ignores it.

```{r eta}
round(fit$eta, 2)
```

## Estimates stored in the fit

`fit$estimates` holds, at the `t2` weights, the coefficients (`coef`),
the ATE over the trial covariates (`ate`), the CATE formula (`cate`)
and, if given covariate values, the CATE there (`cate_at`).

```{r stored}
fit$estimates$coef
fit$estimates$ate
fit$estimates$cate
fit$estimates$cate_at
```

The stored `cate` is a function; call it on covariates to predict the
CATE with intervals (link scale, here the response scale).

```{r cate-fn}
fit$estimates$cate(data.frame(X = c(-1, 0, 3)))
```

Each can be set to `FALSE`. Models whose effect is not linear in the
parameters have no CATE formula; use `mdpl_cate()` there. The functions
below recompute these for other traces, scales, populations and levels.

## CATE, ATE and coefficients

```{r cate}
cbind(nd, truth = 0.2 + 0.1 * nd$X, mdpl_cate(fit, nd)[, -1])
mdpl_ate(fit)
```

`trace = "t1"` gives the more conservative weights.

```{r t1}
mdpl_ate(fit, trace = "t1")
```

`mdpl_ate()` averages the CATE over the trial covariates (or any data
frame). The trial-only fit is `fit$rct`:

```{r rct}
rbind(trial_only = mdpl_ate(fit$rct, trial, treat = "A"),
      mdpl = mdpl_ate(fit))
```

`mdpl_coef()` returns the fused treatment coefficients:

```{r coef}
mdpl_coef(fit)
```

```{r plot}
g <- data.frame(X = seq(-1, 3, length.out = 41))
a <- mdpl_cate(fit, g)
b <- mdpl_cate(fit$rct, g, treat = "A")
plot(NA, xlim = range(g$X), ylim = c(-0.5, 1), xlab = "X", ylab = "CATE")
polygon(c(g$X, rev(g$X)), c(b$lower, rev(b$upper)), col = "#99999940", border = NA)
polygon(c(g$X, rev(g$X)), c(a$lower, rev(a$upper)), col = "#0072B240", border = NA)
lines(g$X, b$estimate, col = "grey40", lwd = 2)
lines(g$X, a$estimate, col = "#0072B2", lwd = 2)
abline(0.2, 0.1, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("truth", "trial only", "MDPL"), lty = c(2, 1, 1), lwd = 2,
       col = c("black", "grey40", "#0072B2"), bty = "n")
```

## Intervals and weights

The intervals above are bootstrap intervals, which account for choosing the
weights. Without `bootstrap_CI = TRUE` they are posterior intervals given the
selected weights, which are narrower; `ci = "posterior"` gives those from this
fit (see the intervals vignette).

## Binary outcomes

Switch the family. Effects are risk differences by default, or log odds
ratios with `scale = "link"`.

```{r binary}
simb <- function(n, bias = 0) {
  X <- rnorm(n); U <- rnorm(n)
  A <- if (bias == 0) rbinom(n, 1, 0.5) else rbinom(n, 1, plogis(X + bias * U))
  data.frame(X = X, A = A,
             Y = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.3 + 0.8 * A + 0.5 * X + 0.3 * A * X + bias * U)))
}
fb <- mdpl(Y ~ A * X, simb(500), list(simb(1500, 0), simb(1500, 1)),
           treat = "A", family = binomial())
fb$eta
nd2 <- data.frame(X = c(-1, 0, 1))
mdpl_cate(fb, nd2)                  # risk difference
mdpl_cate(fb, nd2, scale = "link")  # log odds ratio
mdpl_ate(fb)                        # standardised risk difference
```

The risk difference is nonlinear in the parameters, so its interval
comes from posterior draws.

## Where to go next

- **Models** (`mdpl-models`): GLM families, `causl` frugal models, and
  custom likelihoods.
- **Weights** (`mdpl-weights`): how the weights are chosen, several
  sources, `target`, and the Taylor, ELPD and cross-validation methods.
- **Intervals** (`mdpl-intervals`): posterior and bootstrap intervals.
- **Overlap** (`mdpl-overlap`): what happens when observational data cover different
  covariates from the trial.
- **Frugal CATE** (`mdpl-frugal-cate`): the copula model with `causl`.
